Notorious

/noh-TOR-ee-us/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Notorious means widely known for something bad — famous for a negative quality or deed

Notorious means widely known for something bad. The old harbor town was once notorious for smugglers who slipped past the dock inspectors every night.

Worked Example

That airline is notorious for losing checked luggage, so Maya packs everything she truly needs into her carry-on.

The airline is famous specifically for a bad practice — that negative fame is what notorious means, and it explains why Maya takes precautions.

Antonyms

reputable

esteemed

How Strong Is It? — unpopular → reviled → notorious

unpopular vs. notorious

unpopular vs. notorious: An unpopular policy is disliked, but a notorious one is famous specifically for being bad.

reviled vs. notorious

reviled vs. notorious: Reviled is stronger than notorious — the person or thing is not just known for bad qualities but actively hated.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — not-

Root — not-: known (Latin notus, from noscere, 'to come to know')

Suffix — -orious

Suffix — -orious: full of; characterized by

Put it together

Put it together: Notorious comes from Latin notus, 'known' — literally 'fully known.' Over the centuries the word narrowed, so that today this fame is always for something bad.

Use the root in a new word: notable

Use the root in a new word: notable: Notable — worthy of being known, usually for something good — shares the root: her free-throw percentage showed a notable improvement after a summer of practice.

Root Check

Word Choice

Common / journalistic

Notorious always carries negative fame — a notorious outlaw, a road notorious for accidents. Don't use it for positive fame; that's renowned or celebrated. Its related noun form, infamy, names the state of having that bad reputation.
